'''''Lonicera tatarica''''' is a species of [[honeysuckle]] known by the common name '''Tatarian honeysuckle'''.<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref> Native to Asia, the plant is one of several exotic bush honeysuckles present in North America,<ref>[http://www.na.fs.fed.us/fhp/invasive_plants/weeds/bush_honeysuckle.pdf US Forest Service Weed of the Week]</ref> being considered an [[Invasive species in the United States|invasive species]] there.

==Description==
''Lonicera tatarica'' is a bushy [[shrub]] which may approach {{convert|3|m|frac=2|abbr=off|sp=us}} in height. The twigs can be an array of colors from green to brown with a hollow brown pith. The plant is lined with oval or rounded simple [[leaves]] {{convert|3|to|6|cm|abbr=off|frac=4}} long.<ref name="tktimb">{{Cite book |last1=Turner |first1=Mark |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VLbAAwAAQBAJ |title=Trees & Shrubs of the Pacific Northwest |last2=Kuhlmann |first2=Ellen |date=2014 |publisher=[[Timber Press]] |isbn=978-1-60469-263-1 |edition=1st |location=Portland, OR |pages=308}}</ref> The leaves and stem range from {{Convert|2.5-6.5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long, {{Convert|1.25-2.5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} wide. They are egg shaped and both hairless and toothless.<ref name="tktimb" />

The [[inflorescence]] ranges in color from deep rose to light pink, and can also be white. The petals are typically {{Convert|2-2.5|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}} long, with a slender tube and 2 lips. The upper lip contains 4 lobes, the middle two erect and fused near the base. The white to pink to crimson red flowers are each about {{convert|1.5|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}} long, their [[stamen]]s and [[gynoecium|styles]] protruding. The fruit is a shiny orange or red<ref name="tktimb" /> seed-containing [[berry (botany)|berry]] less than 1'' ''cm wide. The berries are attractive to wildlife.<ref name="NC-Ext-Gard">{{cite web | title=''Lonicera tatarica'' (Tatarian Honeysuckle) | website=[[North Carolina Extension]] Gardener Plant Toolbox | url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/lonicera-tatarica/ | access-date=2021-05-03}}</ref> The plant forms thickets and spreads easily when birds and other animals consume the fruits. The flowers have a sweet smell that is reminiscent of honeysuckle.

In cultivation, ''L. tatarica'' has hybridized with other shrubby species of ''Lonicera''. Crossed with ''[[Lonicera morrowii|L. morrowii]]'', it forms the invasive hybrid [[Lonicera × bella|''L.'' × ''bella'']].<ref name=BarnCott74>{{Cite journal |last1=Barnes |first1=William J. |last2=Cottam |first2=Grant |date=1974 |title=Some Autecological Studies of the ''Lonicera'' × ''bella'' Complex |journal=Ecology |volume=55 |issue=1 |pages=40–50 |jstor=1934616 |name-list-style=amp |doi=10.2307/1934616 |bibcode=1974Ecol...55...40B }}</ref> It can also hybridize with ''[[Lonicera ruprechtiana|L. ruprechtiana]]'' and ''[[Lonicera xylosteum|L. xylosteum]]''.<ref name=Gree66>{{Cite journal |last1=Green |first1=P.S. |date=1966 |title=Identification of the Species and Hybrids in the ''Lonicera tatarica'' Complex |journal=Journal of the Arnold Arboretum |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=75–88 |doi=10.5962/p.324689 |jstor=43781553 |s2cid=240345901 |doi-access=free |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/partpdf/324689 }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''L. tatarica'' is native to [[Siberia]] and other parts of eastern Asia, especially China.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=honeysuckle {{!}} Description & Major Species |url=https://www.britannica.com/plant/honeysuckle |access-date=2021-05-03 |website=Encyclopedia Britannica |language=en}}</ref> It is also known to grow in the Himalayas. After being introduced to North America as an [[ornamental plant]] in 1752,<ref>[https://www.invasive.org/species/subject.cfm?sub=3043 Invasive.org]</ref> became a widespread [[introduced species]] and [[noxious weed]]. It is known across the continent west to [[Alaska]] and [[California]], where it easily grows in disturbed habitat.

Its preferred environment is partial sun with moist, loamy soil. It is also able to grow in full shade or sun, and in dry or sandy soils.

==Ecology==
[[File:Rhagoletis cerasi on Tatarian Honeysuckle (Lonicera tatarica) - Oslo, Norway 2020-08-04 (01).jpg|thumb|''[[Rhagoletis]]'' fruit fly on berry]]

The species threatens native habitats because the plants grow quickly and form thick, impenetrable mats that smother their competitors.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Drummond |first=Brie |date=2005 |title=The Selection of Native and Invasive Plants by Frugivorous Birds in Maine |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/3858501.pdf |journal=Northeastern Naturalist |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=33–44 |doi=10.1656/1092-6194(2005)012[0033:TSONAI]2.0.CO;2 |jstor=3858501 |s2cid=54818044 }}</ref> It most commonly invades thickets, open woodlands, roadsides and fence rows. Animals such as birds and mammals disperse the seeds, causing a rapid spread which often leads to a dense understory thicket that not only restricts native plant growth but also inhibits biodiversity. Once ''L. tatarica'' is introduced into an environment, it is hard to control the growth of the plant in nature because honeysuckles grow at high density. In addition to high densities, ''L. tatarica'' has the ability to suppress the growth of other native plants in the area, thus creating [[Monoculture|monocultures]]. Problems reported with the invasion of ''L. tatarica'' include depletion of soil moisture and nutrients, allelopathic chemicals functioning to chemically alter the growth of native plants, and reductions in the density of tree seedlings in the area.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tatarian Honeysuckle |url=https://www.mda.state.mn.us/plants/pestmanagement/weedcontrol/noxiouslist/tatarianhoneysuckle |access-date=2021-05-03 |website=www.mda.state.mn.us |publisher=Minnesota Department of Agriculture}}</ref>

The wood invokes a behavioural response in about half of domestic cats. Of cats that do not respond to [[catnip]], one third respond to Tatarian honeysuckle.<ref>{{cite journal | pmc=5356310 | year=2017 | last1=Bol | first1=S. | last2=Caspers | first2=J. | last3=Buckingham | first3=L. | last4=Anderson-Shelton | first4=G. D. | last5=Ridgway | first5=C. | last6=Buffington | first6=C. A. | last7=Schulz | first7=S. | last8=Bunnik | first8=E. M. | title=Responsiveness of cats (Felidae) to silver vine (Actinidia polygama), Tatarian honeysuckle (Lonicera tatarica), valerian (Valeriana officinalis) and catnip (Nepeta cataria) | journal=BMC Veterinary Research | volume=13 | issue=1 | page=70 | doi=10.1186/s12917-017-0987-6 | pmid=28302120 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

In its native habitat, Tatarian honeysuckle is a host plant to at least 16 Lepidoptera species, including ''[[Limenitis camilla]]'', ''[[Limenitis helmanni]]'' and ''[[Perittia sibirica]].''<ref>{{Cite web |title=HOSTS – a Database of the World's Lepidopteran Hostplants – Data Portal |url=https://data.nhm.ac.uk/dataset/hosts/resource/877f387a-36a3-486c-a0c1-b8d5fb69f85a?q=lonicera+tatarica&view_id=e2a17eb7-1c7c-4d41-9d95-7c697f5d50ab&field=Damage&value= |access-date=2024-06-08 |website=data.nhm.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref> 

== Toxicity ==
The species has a low poisonous severity level to humans, with no reports of its fatal consumption. Eating its berries is not recommended, causing symptoms including diarrhea, vomiting and abdominal pain.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Lonicera tatarica (Tatarian Honeysuckle) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/lonicera-tatarica/|access-date=2021-05-03|website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref>
